Q: How to get total revenues per customer A:

I don't know whether you mean "revenue" in the accounting sense or "payment volume" or "MRR". These are very different numbers.

Here's a simple scenario with a refund taken from What is revenue?:

Imagine that $1,200/year customer cancels at the end of February and gets a full refund:

  • Payment Volume: Swings wildly from $1,200 (Jan) to -$1,200 (Feb).

  • MRR: Show $100 for both Jan and Feb.

  • Revenue: Accurately shows $100 for Jan (service delivered) and -$100 for Feb (reversing the earned amount).

If you want payment volume, you can download the report called "itemized balance report".

Q: Building a Stripe Sigma query for revenue recognition on subscriptions A:

I don't think we can calculate revenue recognition using a Sigma SQL, certainly not based on subscription.

The main blocker is that you'll have to consider refunds, disputes, credit notes, void, and mark uncollectible and subtract revenue.

Stripe offers Stripe Revenue Recognition (paid with free trial) or you can install Book of Revenue (free); both apps calculate debits & credits of each transaction, offer revenue, deferred revenue, customer liabilities, tax liabilities, and etc. Those things are connected, so it would be weird to just calculate revenue.

Q: What is a scalable alternative to embedding-based skill canonicalization in an ATS system A:

For short skill names, I’d avoid embeddings as the primary canonicalization layer. Normalize first, then use an alias/taxonomy mapping for known skills and fuzzy matching (e.g. RapidFuzz or pg_trgm) for unresolved variants.

For scale, cache canonical mappings and review only low-confidence matches. This keeps matching deterministic and low-latency while allowing new skills to be added incrementally.

Q: Computer programs from the point of view of CPU A:

"Your feelings serve you well".

The key thing concept here is "should follow a similar pattern " - but what actually generates the instructions the CPUs will run, the "machine code" is the compiler.

So, not only the language: C, C++, Go, Rust, Zig, pascal - but which compiler you are using, which flags to the compiler and which compiler version: all of then will change the final machine code. There is the 'Assembler' language which maps almost 1:1 with to the instructions the CPU will execute, and is used as "human readable form" for those instructions. You can ultimately findout the "disassembly" of your alogorithm after it is compiled in different languages to check that. For example, you could run the same 'find root square for a vector of 100 numbers", in the same language, same compiler, but one version compiled to use just the main CPU, and the other version with compiler flags to make use of SIMD CPU Extensions (Single Instruction Multiple Data vector maths - like SSE and AVX): the second version will have a very different assembler, and run much faster, even the source file being the same.

Keep in mind that other category of languages won't run directly on the CPU by default (and even those I listed will not necessarily run directly on the CPU): languages like Python, Java, Ruby, PHP have their code translated into a 'virtual machine bytecode': an "assembler form" which doesn't map directly to the CPU instructions and registers, and those languages depend on the language runtime to interpret that bytecode as they run. Still, most of those will be able to show you their "virtual assembler code", whih is structurally similar to the native assembler for the CPU - but won't name directly registers and memory operations.

Q: Learning about Java bytecode and the JVM A:

I learned by reading the ASM tutorial and mucking about with the library itself.

IMHO, ASM is better than BECL.

BCEL is already being used successfully in several projects such as compilers, optimizers, obsfuscators, code generators and analysis tools. Unfortunately there hasn't been much development going on over the past few years. Feel free to help out or you might want to have a look into the ASM project at objectweb. - http://jakarta.apache.org/bcel/
